claims.text: The starting coating has an FCC matrix interspersed with BCC regions.
The FCC/BCC phase boundaries are coherent or semi-coherent and have controlled lattice misfit.
Stable FCC/BCC phase boundaries are the governing factor responsible for creep resistance.
Lattice distortion at FCC/BCC phase boundaries produces localized elastic strain fields.
Lattice distortion impedes continuous or long-range dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation glide delays the formation of shear bands.
Stable FCC/BCC phase boundaries promote non-Schmid slip behavior.
Promoting non-Schmid slip disperses strain and prevents plastic-strain localization.
Higher FCC/BCC lattice misfit disrupts the phase boundaries or makes them less stable.
Interfacial lattice misfit affects creep behavior.
Increasing lattice misfit reduces the dislocation-barrier effect and accelerates creep.
Under sustained loading, the baseline coating will have a lower creep strain rate than the coating with altered phase boundaries.
Under sustained loading, the baseline coating will form fewer or smaller shear bands than the altered-boundary variant.
The proposed mechanism operates only while temperature and stress remain low enough to preserve phase-interface integrity.
Conditions causing phase decomposition or excessive coarsening fall outside the mechanism's operating boundaries.
Prior microstructural observations support a qualitative role for FCC/BCC phase-boundary stability in creep resistance.
The quantitative effects of phase-boundary stability on creep rate and dislocation dynamics remain undetermined.
Comparable creep rates and microstructural stability in the altered-boundary and baseline coatings would falsify the claim that stable FCC/BCC boundaries govern creep resistance.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the boundaries impede continuous dislocation glide, explicitly including non-Schmid slip, whereas the mechanism says the same boundaries promote non-Schmid slip.

The mechanism treats promoted non-Schmid slip as strain-dispersing and shear-band-suppressing, but the cited non-Schmid evidence reports that non-Schmid slip promotes slip continuity, strain localization, and shear-band formation.
